https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government waives farm fees, expands cancer screening and bans circus animals The government also made decisions on strengthening the independence of the agricultural chamber, the election process for the president and deputies of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), measures to ensure the transparency of public funds, free driving licence acquisition for those in child protection care, and the establishment of a more effective screening system for cancer — government spokespersons announced at a press conference on Friday. Government spokesperson Anita Köböl stated that due to natural disasters in recent times — such as nationwide frost damage and drought, as well as livestock epidemics — the government supports an individual parliamentary motion under which the chamber may waive the collection of membership fees. This step amounts to an overall relief of approximately 18.6 billion forints for more than 400,000 producers, Anita Köböl highlighted. She added that, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, the funds are available, so this assistance does not jeopardise the balance of the budget. The government spokesperson also said that, in the government’s view, Hungarian agriculture is in immediate need of liquidity assistance and long-term protection. By the end of July, damage reports had been submitted for more than 768,000 hectares, which is more than double last year’s figure. She noted that, due to pressure on purchase prices, dairy farmers have also found themselves in a persistently difficult situation. For this reason, she announced, the agricultural minister has been tasked by the government with developing a comprehensive, long-term agricultural strategy. He indicated that the ministry will assist farmers who have suffered unprecedented elemental damage in 2026 by using available resources to pay out a so-called super advance. Instead of the usual mid-October date, payments will be launched as early as September, and the advance rate will be raised from 70 percent to 75 percent. Anita Köböl also reported that the cabinet had decided to further strengthen the transparency of public spending. She said that one of the conditions for accessing the resources of the European Union’s recovery fund is that public bodies involved in using these funds must proactively publish this data in a central registry. She indicated that the decision will expand the range of those obligated to publish and the data required to be disclosed, which will be freely accessible to anyone. “The use of public funds must be made traceable for everyone. Citizens have the right to know who the state is contracting with, what it is spending money on, and who receives the amounts paid from public funds,” she said. Anita Köböl also spoke about the government having instructed the Minister of Health to establish a far more effective and broader screening system accessible to all. The government spokesperson explained that a significant proportion of cancer deaths could be prevented, and a screening system that functions better, more accurately, and more predictably could save thousands of Hungarians every year. However, the latest data show that the participation rate of the Hungarian population in organised screening programmes is not only low but is continuously declining. She stressed that the government had therefore adopted a proposal on the review of the public health screening system and the preparation of its development. The Minister of Health and the Prime Minister will also take part in the available screenings in order to lead by example, she added. The acquisition, breeding, keeping, training, exhibition, and use of certain defined wild animal species and their hybrids in circus performances will be prohibited after 1 January 2027, government spokesperson Éva Magyar announced. She explained that in recent years there had been increasingly strong societal and animal welfare expectations that wild animals should not be used in circus productions. The trend across Europe is also clear, with member states restricting or banning the use of wild animals in circuses, she stressed. He touched on the fact that Hungary had previously applied only a partial ban, which had allowed animals from countries with stricter regulations to be brought into Hungarian menageries. He described the decision as justified on both animal welfare and safety grounds, pointing out that the keeping, transportation, training, and public performance of wild animals is incompatible with modern animal welfare standards and can also pose a risk of accidents. The regulation provides a fair transition: animals lawfully kept at the time of entry into force may continue to be kept for the rest of their lives or for as long as they remain part of the menagerie, but may not be bred, trained, displayed, or used in circus performances, the government spokesperson stated. Photograph: Joe Daniel Price/Getty Images New York New York City police fatally shoot man who climbed up Brooklyn Bridge cables Officers clipped to bridge had tried to talk man, who was holding a knife, into coming down safely, officials say Anna Betts Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.25 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New York City police shot and killed a man on Friday morning after he climbed on to the cables of the Brooklyn Bridge and approached officers with a knife extended, New York police department officials said. At a news conference on Friday, NYPD officials said that a 911 call came in at around 3.28am on Friday morning, reporting that a man was walking on the beams of the Brooklyn Bridge. Officers with the NYPD’s emergency service unit (ESU) responded to the scene, and saw a man “walking on the bridge cables”, Gerald Dowling, the commanding officer of ESU, told reporters. “Members of ESU climbed on to those cables and attempted to establish a verbal dialogue with the male and safely remove him from the bridge,” Dowling said. Dowling noted that the officers spent almost an hour speaking with the man, explaining that they were there to help, and tried to convince him to get down from the bridge safely. During the interaction, the officers observed that the man was holding a knife, he said. The man told the officers: “I want to die, I want you to kill me. I have a bomb. You are not going to make me do something bad to the cops.” Throughout the interaction, Dowling said, the officers continued trying to convince him to get down safely, while also issuing “multiple verbal commands for him to drop the knife”. After about an hour, hundreds of feet above the East River, the man “began to quickly descend the cable of the bridge towards the officers”, Dowling said, adding that at the time, the officers were still clipped to the bridge and positioned below the man on the same cable. Dowling said that when ESU officers are “conducting high-angle rescue”, they wear safety gear, including a harness, which is “physically clipped into the bridge” for their safety and noted that “being secured to the bridge drastically impacts the speed of their movement”. “The officers began to move backwards away from the male, but they were not able to move as quickly as the subject who was approaching them,” Dowling said. “When the male got within approximately 3ft from the closest member of ESU, he raised his arm with the knife extended outward towards the officer.” At that point, Dowling said, an ESU officer “who was on the roadbed of the bridge discharged his weapon one time, striking the male”. Dowling said that the officers then brought the male down from the cable and began rendering aid. The man was transported to a local hospital where he was pronounced deceased. A knife and a flashlight were recovered from the scene. Officials said that the entire incident was captured on police-worn body cameras. On social media, the police shared a photo of what they said was the knife recovered from the scene. The police have not yet released details regarding the identity of the man. “This incident is being investigated by the force investigation division,” Dowling said. “Members of ESU are specially trained for these types of high-risk and incredibly dangerous situations. They receive extensive instruction on de-escalation and how to engage with individuals compassionately.” The shooting came several days after police shot and killed a woman in Times Square after she attacked two people with knives, killing a 32-year-old woman .
